index.title: Articles for newcomers to Canada | MapleSteps
index.desc: Practical, step-by-step articles for newcomers to Canada: health cards, bank accounts, driver's licences and your first winter.
index.lead: Detailed answers to common questions, with the exact steps and the official pages to use.

health-card.title: How to get your provincial health card as a newcomer | MapleSteps
health-card.desc: How newcomers get a provincial health card in Canada: who qualifies, waiting periods by province, what to bring, and how to stay covered while you wait.
health-card.h1: How to get your provincial health card
health-card.summary: Who qualifies, which provinces make you wait, what to bring, and how to stay covered in the meantime.
health-card.lead: In Canada, public health insurance is run by each province and territory. Your health card lets you see a doctor or go to hospital without paying for medically necessary care. Apply in the first days after you arrive.

sections.h: Who can get a health card
items: Permanent residents and Canadian citizens who live in the province
Many work permit holders, depending on the province and how long the permit lasts
Some international students, depending on the province (others must buy school health insurance)
Protected persons and resettled refugees
Ontario has no waiting period. Coverage can start as soon as you are eligible and apply.
Most other provinces, including British Columbia, Quebec and Alberta, can make newcomers wait up to about three months.
During the wait you pay for any care yourself, and a hospital visit can cost thousands of dollars.
Buy private newcomer or visitor health insurance to cover this gap. Some plans must be bought within a few days of arrival, so do it early.
Your immigration document: Confirmation of Permanent Residence (COPR), PR card or valid work or study permit
Proof of your address in the province, such as a lease, bank statement or utility bill
A second ID with your name and signature, such as your passport
Each province publishes its exact list. Check it before you go, because Ontario, for example, asks for three original documents.
Ontario: in person at a ServiceOntario centre
British Columbia: online with Health Insurance BC
Quebec: with the RAMQ (Régie de l'assurance maladie du Québec)
Alberta: at a registry agent office or online
Other provinces: on the provincial health ministry website

sections.p: Resettled refugees and refugee claimants who are not yet covered by their province may get temporary coverage from the federal government through the Interim Federal Health Program (IFHP). Ask your settlement worker or the clinic to check your eligibility.

bank-account.title: Opening your first Canadian bank account as a newcomer | MapleSteps
bank-account.desc: How newcomers open a bank account in Canada: your rights, the ID you need, newcomer account offers, deposit insurance and how to avoid fees and scams.
bank-account.h1: Opening your first Canadian bank account
bank-account.summary: Your rights, the ID you need, what newcomer packages offer, and how your money is protected.
bank-account.lead: A Canadian bank account is one of the first things you need. Employers pay salaries by direct deposit, landlords often want rent by e-transfer, and the government pays benefits into your account.

sections.h: You have the right to an account
items: You don't need a job, a credit history or money to deposit to open a personal bank account.
You don't need to be a Canadian citizen or permanent resident, but you may need to go to a branch in person.
A bank can refuse only for specific reasons, such as fraud. If it refuses, it must tell you in writing and explain how to complain.
Option 1: two original documents from the bank's list, for example your passport and your Confirmation of Permanent Residence or permit.
Option 2: one document with your name and date of birth, plus a person in good standing (for example an existing customer) who confirms who you are.
Bring originals, not copies. Your Social Insurance Number (SIN) is needed for accounts that earn interest.
Most big banks and many credit unions offer newcomer packages, often with no monthly fee for the first year and a starter credit card.
Since December 1, 2025, most large banks must offer newcomers a no-cost account for their first year in Canada, and anyone can get a low-cost account for $4 a month or less.
Check what happens after the first year: the monthly fee, the number of free transactions, and e-transfer charges.
A chequing account is for daily spending. A savings account earns a little interest.
Online banks often have no monthly fees, but may have fewer services for newcomers.
Use the free Account Comparison Tool from the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada to compare monthly fees, free transactions and interest across banks side by side.
Deposits at member banks are insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC) up to $100,000 per category, per bank.
Categories include accounts in your own name, joint accounts, TFSAs and RRSPs. Credit unions are protected by provincial insurers.
Never share your PIN, online banking password or one-time codes. Banks never ask for them by phone or text.

sections.p: Bank wire transfers can be expensive. Compare the total cost, including the exchange rate, with money transfer services before you send. Always use a licensed company and never send money to someone you only know online.

drivers-licence.title: Getting your driver's licence as a newcomer to Canada | MapleSteps
drivers-licence.desc: How newcomers get a driver's licence in Canada: exchanging a foreign licence, getting credit for experience, Ontario's 60-day rule, and car insurance tips.
drivers-licence.h1: Getting your driver's licence in Canada
drivers-licence.summary: Exchanging your foreign licence, getting credit for experience, and why you need to act within weeks.
drivers-licence.lead: Each province issues its own driver's licences, and the rules for newcomers differ. Some countries' licences can be exchanged directly; others mean taking tests. Start early, because your foreign licence is only valid for a short time once you live here.

items: In Ontario, new residents must apply for an Ontario licence within 60 days. After that, the foreign licence can no longer be used.
Other provinces have similar time limits, often around 90 days. Check your province's rule as soon as you arrive.

Ontario exchanges licences from other provinces, U.S. states and some countries, including Australia, France, Germany, Ireland, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan, Ukraine and the United Kingdom.
For a full G licence, you need proof of at least two years of driving experience within the last three years.
Without enough proof, you get a beginner licence and go through Ontario's graduated licensing steps.

sections.h: If your country has no agreement
items: You can get credit for up to 12 months of experience, which can shorten the beginner stage.
In Ontario, from July 1, 2026, drivers in this group take the G2 road test, then the G road test at least 12 months later.
You still take the written knowledge test and a vision test.
Get a letter of authentication from your home country's licensing office, embassy or consulate.
In Ontario it must be issued within the last six months and show your first licence date, class, status and expiry date.
Documents not in English or French need a translation by a recognized translator. Bring originals, because the office may keep them.

sections.p: Insurance is mandatory and can be very expensive for drivers with no Canadian history. Ask insurers whether they accept a letter from your home-country insurer showing your claims-free years, and compare several quotes before you buy a car.

first-winter.title: Your first Canadian winter: what to buy and what to skip | MapleSteps
first-winter.desc: A newcomer's guide to the first Canadian winter: how to dress in layers, what boots and coats to buy, wind chill safety, saving money and staying well.
first-winter.summary: How to dress for the cold, what's worth buying, what you can skip, and how to stay safe and well.
first-winter.lead: Canadian winters are long and, in most cities, very cold. With the right clothing, life carries on normally: buses run, children go to school and people go outside. The secret is layers, not one huge coat.

items: Base layer: thin thermal top and leggings that keep moisture away from your skin. Avoid cotton, which stays wet.
Middle layer: a fleece or wool sweater to hold warmth.
Outer layer: a windproof, waterproof coat that covers your hips. A hood helps a lot.
Layers let you take one off indoors, where buildings are warm.
Insulated, waterproof boots with good grip. Wet, cold feet ruin a winter day, and sidewalks get icy.
A warm hat that covers your ears, a scarf or neck warmer, and insulated gloves or mittens (mittens are warmer).
Wool socks, two or three pairs.
If you drive: winter tires, an ice scraper and a snow brush. Quebec requires winter tires by law from December 1 to March 15.

sections.h: What you can skip or buy cheaply
items: Expensive designer parkas: a mid-priced coat with layers underneath is enough for most cities.
Buy children's winter gear secondhand. They outgrow it every year.
Thrift stores and online marketplaces sell good coats and boots for much less, especially in the fall.
Ask your settlement agency about free winter clothing programs. Many communities run coat drives.
Weather forecasts show a temperature and a wind chill, which is how cold it feels on your skin.
Environment Canada warns that frostbite risk rises quickly when the wind chill is below -27.
On very cold days, cover exposed skin and limit time outside. Watch for white or numb patches on fingers, ears and nose.
Check the forecast on the Government of Canada weather site or app each morning.

sections.h: Stay well in the dark months
sections.p: Days are short from November to February. Go outside in daylight when you can, stay active, and keep in touch with friends and family. Feeling low in winter is common. If it lasts, talk to a doctor, or call or text 988 if you are in crisis.

switch-banks.title: How to switch banks in Canada when your newcomer offer ends | MapleSteps
switch-banks.desc: How to switch banks in Canada (or change banks) when your free newcomer package ends: check the date, get a free or $4 account, compare no-fee banks and move your money step by step.
switch-banks.h1: Your newcomer bank offer is ending: how to avoid fees or switch banks
switch-banks.sub: What to do 6 to 12 months after opening your first account
switch-banks.summary: Check when your free period ends, ask for a cheaper plan, or move your money step by step without missed payments.
switch-banks.lead: Many newcomer bank packages are free for the first year. After that, monthly fees start, often without much warning. Here is how to keep your costs low, whether you stay with your bank or move.

sections.h: Find out when your offer ends
items: Look at the welcome letter or account agreement from when you opened the account. Most newcomer packages last about 12 months.
After the offer ends, the account usually moves to a regular plan, which can cost about $10 to $30 a month.
Set a reminder one month before the end date, and check your statement for a new monthly fee line.

sections.h: Ask your bank for a cheaper plan first
items: Since December 1, 2025, most large banks must offer anyone a low-cost chequing account for $4 a month or less, with at least 18 debit transactions and no minimum balance.
The same banks must offer a no-cost account to newcomers in their first year in Canada, students, youth, seniors receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement and RDSP beneficiaries.
Ask whether keeping a minimum balance would waive your monthly fee, and how much it is.
Changing to another account at the same bank is usually simpler than switching banks, and low-cost account rules say there is no fee for it.
Online banks often have no monthly fee, but may have fewer branches and services for newcomers.
Credit unions are member-owned local institutions. Many offer low-fee accounts and personal service.
Compare the costs you will really pay: e-transfers, ATM withdrawals, cards used abroad and sending money home.
Check that a bank is a CDIC member, or that a credit union is covered by its provincial deposit insurer.
Use the free Account Comparison Tool from the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada to compare monthly fees, free transactions and interest across banks side by side.

sections.h: How to switch banks, step by step
items: Open the new account first. Don't close the old one until everything has moved.
Give your new account details to your employer for direct deposit, and update your banking information with the Canada Revenue Agency for tax refunds and benefits.
Make a list of pre-authorized payments, such as rent, phone, internet, insurance, gym and subscriptions, and move each one.
Stop writing cheques from the old account and wait until any cheques you wrote have been cashed.
Watch both accounts for a month or two. When nothing is left, move the remaining money and close the old account, and ask for written confirmation.
Some banks charge a fee if you close an account soon after opening it. Ask before you close.
If you received a cash bonus, check its conditions. Closing the account too early can mean paying it back.
A payment taken from an empty or closed account can lead to a non-sufficient funds (NSF) fee.
Bank accounts do not affect your credit score, but credit cards do. If your newcomer package included a credit card with no annual fee, keeping it open can help your credit history.
Never share your PIN, passwords or one-time codes, even with someone who says they are helping you switch.

sections.p: In Budget 2025, the federal government said it will work with banks to make moving a chequing account to another institution simpler and will review fees such as e-transfer and ATM charges. No dates have been set yet, so check the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada for updates.

credit-history.title: How to build a credit history in Canada as a newcomer | MapleSteps
credit-history.desc: Your credit history from home usually doesn't count in Canada. How credit scores work, how to get your first credit card, and the habits that build good credit in your first year.
credit-history.h1: Building a credit history in Canada
credit-history.summary: Why your credit from home doesn't count, how scores work, and the habits that build good credit in your first year.
credit-history.lead: In Canada, landlords, phone companies, car dealers and lenders often check your credit before saying yes. Credit history from another country usually doesn't carry over, so most newcomers start from zero. With a few simple habits, you can build a solid record within your first year.

items: Landlords may check your credit before renting to you. A thin record can mean a larger deposit or a request for a co-signer.
Phone plans, car loans, mortgages and some insurance prices can depend on your credit.
Some employers check credit for jobs that handle money, but only with your permission.
The earlier you start, the better, because the length of your history counts.
Canada has two credit bureaus, Equifax and TransUnion. Each keeps its own report about you, so the two can differ.
Scores range from 300 to 900. Higher is better.
Having no Canadian history is not the same as having bad credit. You simply have no score yet, until lenders start reporting your accounts.
Your score depends mainly on paying on time, how much of your credit limit you use, how long you have had credit, and how often you apply for new credit.
A bank account alone does not build credit. Only credit products, such as credit cards and loans, are reported to the bureaus.
Many big banks offer newcomer credit cards that don't need a Canadian credit history, often as part of a newcomer banking package. Ask your own bank first.

If you are refused, a secured credit card is a good start. You give a deposit, for example $500, and that becomes your limit. You get the deposit back when you close the card or move to a regular card.
Choose a card with no annual fee. You don't need rewards to build credit.
Prepaid cards look like credit cards but do not build credit. Check that your card reports to Equifax and TransUnion.
Pay on time, every time. Late payments can stay on your credit report for years.
Pay the full balance each month if you can. If not, always pay at least the minimum. Credit card interest is often around 20% a year.
Use less than 30% of your limit. On a $1,000 limit, try to keep the balance under $300.
Set up an automatic payment for at least the minimum, so you never miss a due date.
Don't apply for many cards or loans at once. Each application can lower your score a little for a while.
Keep your oldest card open, even if you use it rarely. Older accounts help your score.

sections.h: Check your credit report for free
items: You can see your credit report online for free from both Equifax and TransUnion, updated monthly. Equifax also shows your score for free.
Checking your own report or score does not lower it.
The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada recommends checking your report from both bureaus at least once a year.
Look for accounts you don't recognise or wrong information. You have the right to dispute errors, and the bureaus must correct them for free.
Many banking apps also show a free credit score.
Payday loans and high-interest instalment loans are very expensive and are not a good way to build credit.
Be careful with companies that promise to fix or build your credit fast for a fee. No one can remove accurate information from your report.
Never let someone else use your name or Social Insurance Number for a loan or phone contract. If they don't pay, your credit suffers.
Co-signing a loan makes you fully responsible if the other person stops paying.
Does my credit score from my home country count in Canada? Usually not. Canadian lenders look at your Canadian credit report, so your record starts with your first Canadian credit product.
Do I have to give my Social Insurance Number for a credit check? Many lenders ask for it, but it is usually optional for a credit check. Ask which other ID they accept.
Does paying rent or my phone bill build credit? Usually not on its own. Most everyday bills only appear on your report if you stop paying and the debt goes to a collection agency.
Can my spouse and I share one credit history? No. Each person has their own credit report, so each of you needs to build credit in your own name.

sections.p: Most newcomers who use a credit card responsibly see a score appear within a few months and build a fair record within six months to a year. Be patient: steady, on-time payments matter more than anything else.

links: Getting your credit report and credit score (FCAC)

send-money.title: How to send money home from Canada for less | MapleSteps
send-money.desc: Sending money abroad from Canada: compare banks and transfer services, spot hidden exchange-rate costs, check that a company is registered with FINTRAC, and avoid scams.
send-money.summary: How to compare the real cost, choose a safe service and make sure your family receives the money.
send-money.lead: Sending money to family is one of the first things many newcomers do. The cost can vary a lot between services, and the biggest cost is often hidden in the exchange rate, not the fee. Here is how to compare and send safely.

items: Banks and credit unions can send an international wire transfer. It is safe, but fees are often higher.
Money transfer companies send money through apps, websites and agents to a bank account, a mobile wallet or for cash pickup. They are often cheaper and faster for common destinations.
Some money transfer businesses also have counters in grocery stores, pharmacies, post offices and convenience stores.
Choose based on how your family can actually receive the money: a bank deposit, a mobile wallet or a cash pickup point near them.
The total cost has three parts: the transfer fee, the exchange rate, and any fee your family pays to collect the money.
A transfer with no fee is not always cheaper. Some businesses make their profit by giving you a worse exchange rate.
The easiest way to compare: ask each service how much your family will receive, in their currency, for the same amount you send.
Check the offered rate against the rate shown on a currency or news website. The closer it is, the less you pay.
Fees can change with the amount, and some services give discounts for larger or repeat transfers.
Paying from your bank account, for example by Interac e-Transfer or debit, is usually the cheapest way.
Paying by credit card may cost more. It can be treated as a cash advance, with interest starting right away at a higher rate.
Faster delivery usually costs more. If it isn't urgent, a slower option can save money.
Ask whether the exchange rate is fixed when you pay or when your family collects the money.

Money transfer companies in Canada must register with FINTRAC, the federal financial intelligence agency. Before you send, look up the company's name and status in FINTRAC's public Money Services Business Registry.
Registration does not guarantee good service, so also ask family, friends and your community about their experience with a company.
Banks and credit unions are regulated and must have a process for complaints.
Some countries are under Canadian sanctions or have banking restrictions. Ask the provider before you send: they may refuse or ask for more information.
Always get a receipt and a transaction number, so you can trace the transfer if something goes wrong.
Ask how you will know the money arrived, and give your family the transaction number and the exact sender name.
Never send money to someone you only know online or by phone, or to pay a fee to release a prize, job, loan or immigration document. These are common scams.
Government agencies such as the CRA and IRCC will never ask you to pay with money transfers, gift cards or cryptocurrency.
FINTRAC never contacts members of the public to ask for financial or personal information.
If your family's needs allow, send larger amounts less often to pay fewer fees.
Compare two or three services each time. The cheapest one can change by country and amount.
Services with offices or partners in both countries may offer lower-cost options.
Keep your receipts. They help if you ever need to show where your money went.
Is there a tax on sending money abroad from Canada? Canada does not charge a tax for sending your own money abroad. Your family may face fees or rules in their country.

Is there a limit on how much I can send? Each service sets its own limits. For larger amounts, the provider may ask where the money comes from. This is normal under Canada's anti-money-laundering rules.
How long does a transfer take? From a few minutes to a few days, depending on the service, the country and how your family receives the money.
Can I cancel a transfer? Sometimes, if the money has not been picked up or deposited yet. Contact the service right away and have your transaction number ready.
